extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO examiners, and legal scholars (patent attorneys, law professors)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing patent subject-matter eligibility under the Alice/Mayo two-step framework (with attention to Federal Circuit case law and USPTO MPEP guidance), especially for software and AI-related inventions. Focuses on how to determine whether claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea and whether they contain an 'inventive concept.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern as the driving consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘driv[ing]’ concern of the eligibility exceptions is preemption — the prospect that a patent would render too much activity infringing; courts must scrutinize patents that would excessively preempt ideas because they risk impeding innovation rather than promoting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim would ‘tie up’ or preempt the basic tools of scientific and technological work. Even if an invention involves ideas (as all do), ask whether the claim scope would ‘render too much activity infringing.’ Absence of total preemption is relevant but insufficient by itself to show eligibility (courts have held that absence of complete preemption does not demonstrate patent eligibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step framework (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step one: determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible abstract idea; if not, the invention is eligible. Step two: if directed to an abstract idea, determine whether the claim contains an ‘inventive concept’ sufficient to ‘transform the nature of the claim[s]’ into a patent-eligible application; if not, the claim is ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the two steps sequentially. Recognize ambiguities in both steps (e.g., what it means to be ‘directed to’ an abstract idea, and what qualifies as an ‘inventive concept’). Use case law (Alice, Mayo, Diehr, and subsequent Federal Circuit decisions) to guide characterization of abstract ideas and inventive concepts. There is no further ‘step three.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Step one — ‘directed to’ an abstract idea / claim ‘focus’ inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: At step one a court asks whether the claims are ‘directed to’ a patent-ineligible concept by looking at the ‘focus’ of the claims — whether they are aimed at an abstract idea or at a specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities or technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the claim’s focus is a specific technological advance (which favors eligibility) or an abstract result/idea (which favors ineligibility). Interpret ‘directed to’ as more than mere presence/containment of an idea. Use precedent (Enfish, Bandai/McRO, Finjan, Elec. Power) to decide whether claims are focused on a specific technical improvement or merely automate a known manual/mental process or effect. Consider examples: McRO/Bandai (eligible because focused on a specific algorithmic rule set improving animation) vs. generic automation of loan applications or virus screening (treated as abstract).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories and limits of abstract ideas (as articulated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts group abstract ideas into categories (e.g., fundamental economic practices; certain methods of organizing human activity; an idea ‘of itself’; mathematical relationships/formulas), and the USPTO (MPEP) later summarized categories as mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a claim recites an abstract idea, map the claimed subject matter to these categories. Be aware that the MPEP attempts to limit examiners to these categories and presumes against finding abstract ideas outside them — but courts have not held those to be the only possible categories. If an examiner contemplates treating an idea as an abstract idea outside these categories, supervisory approval may be required (per MPEP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three claim-types that almost always fail Alice step one
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit has identified three claim types that almost always fail step one: (1) claims that simply demand the production of a desired result (no limitation on how achieved); (2) claims to processes that can be performed in the human mind (or their automatic equivalents); (3) claims that gather and analyze information of a specified content and then display the results, when done in a conventional way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for broadly preemptive result-oriented claims, mental-process-equivalent claims, and conventional data-collection/analysis/display claims. These raise heightened preemption concerns and typically proceed to step two, where they often fail absent a transformative inventive concept. Use these categories as red flags during drafting/examination and argue specificity or technical solution if seeking eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step two — ‘inventive concept’ requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to an abstract idea at step one, courts must search for an ‘inventive concept’ — claim elements beyond the abstract idea that ‘transform’ the claim into a patent-eligible application; token invocations of generic computer parts or instructions to ‘apply it’ will not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for claim elements that meaningfully limit the abstract idea so preemption is avoided. Factors supporting an inventive concept include: use of nongeneric or specially adapted technology; a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known components; absence of total preemption; presence of a technical improvement; and a technical solution to a problem unique to a particular technological context. Case law examples: BASCOM (claims eligible at step two due to specific location and customizable filtering features and lack of total preemption); Diehr (technical improvement via continuous temperature measurement). The bar is high; many claims fail at step two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical improvement / ‘technical solution to a technical problem’ as the most important factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that represent a technical solution to a technical problem (i.e., a specific asserted improvement to computers or technology) are more likely to be found eligible at one or both steps of Alice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting or evaluating claims, emphasize how the invention improves computer functionality or solves a technology-specific problem (not merely makes a process more efficient by automation). Courts treat specificity of the improvement as important — mere novelty, brilliance, or general improvement is not enough; the claimed improvement must be specific and tied to limitations that reduce preemption concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined (step-zero) analysis in USPTO guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO’s streamlined eligibility analysis is a fast track to eligibility where the invention ‘clearly’ does not preempt an idea or ‘clearly improve[s] a technology or computer functionality,’ allowing examiners to presume eligibility without full two-step analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the 2019 MPEP changes, examiners may use streamlined analysis for claims showing clear technological improvement (citing Bandai and Enfish fact patterns). Be cautious: courts require detailed analysis of preemption and specificity; the mere appearance of an improvement does not guarantee eligibility. The Office’s adoption of broadened streamlined analysis departs in some respects from judicial precedent and can be contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP’s addition of a second prong within step one: ‘integration into a practical application’
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites a judicial exception, examiners should consider whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (e.g., an apparent improvement to computers disclosed in specification/claims); if so, the claim may be eligible without proceeding to step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration requires more than conclusory assertions of improvement — the improvement should be apparent from the specification and claims. This is an MPEP-specific placement of the search for technological improvement at an earlier point in the analysis; courts typically look for technical improvements at step one, step two, or both. Emphasize specificity and reduced preemption when arguing integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional computer automation / improved efficiency alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficiency gains that result only from computer automation — i.e., using a computer ‘merely as a tool’ to perform a known manual process more efficiently — do not amount to an improvement to computers themselves and are not enough to establish eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between inventions that improve computer functionality/architecture and those that merely automate tasks. Claims that only capture improved speed or convenience of automating a manual process typically fail Alice. Use claim language to tie inventions to changes in computer operation or architecture where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity requirement and limits of ‘absence of total preemption’
rubrics_metrics.description: Specificity in claimed improvements matters because it reduces preemption; conversely, absence of total preemption (i.e., not tying up the entire idea) alone does not establish eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or drafting claims, identify precise means, methods, or structural limitations that limit the claim’s scope. Courts look for specific means or methods that improve technology rather than broad results. The MPEP’s emphasis on ‘improvement’ should be accompanied by claims and specification that demonstrate particularity and specific technical features to withstand eligibility scrutiny.
